interactions.summary: The reading continues the eagle passage through Trajan, William, and Rhipeus, after which Jiang stops on Rhipeus as the hardest salvation paradox.
A student says everyone can make it if they really will it, and Jiang pushes back until the class lands on intuition for the good as enough to move toward heaven.

claims.claim: Jiang treats Rhipeus as a more radical salvation case than Statius because Rhipeus lived before Jesus and even before Hebrew revelation.
Jiang rejects a simplistic will-only answer by noting that Rhipeus could not consciously choose a heaven or Christ he never historically knew.
The class position Jiang ratifies is that one can still follow intuition toward what is good and right without doctrinal knowledge of heaven.

signature_moments.moment: Rhipeus explodes the gatekeeping logic because he predates the institutions that were supposed to be necessary.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the textual wedge Jiang uses to break Virgil’s rule that only explicit Christians can enter heaven.

signature_moments.moment: The path to heaven is recast as fidelity to the good before it is doctrinally named.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you can still follow your intuition and know what's good and right
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the compact democratic salvation formula the class arrives at.

chronology_notes.note: This packet records Jiang’s June 26 movement from explicit conversion toward a more universal account of salvation through righteousness and intuition.
